title: SYSK’s Fall True Crime Playlist: The Tylenol Murders, Part I
summary: Part one of a two-part Stuff You Should Know episode on the 1982 Tylenol murders in the Chicago area. Hosts open with banter about 1982 news events, then describe the deaths of seven people beginning September 29, 1982: Mary Anne Kellerman, Adam Janis, Mary Reiner, Mary McFarlane, Stanley Janis, Teresa Janis (who survived a couple of days), and Paula Prince, all linked to extra strength Tylenol capsules laced with potassium cyanide. They explain cyanide's effects, the role of medical examiner Michael Schaeffer, fire captain Philip Capitelli, public health nurse Helen Jensen, Cook County deputy chief medical examiner Edmund Donahue's press conference, Mayor Jane Byrne's response, the Tylenol Task Force, copycat tampering incidents and hoaxes, and the investigators' conclusion that the tampering happened in local stores (the "mad poisoner" theory) with lot MC2880 found clean. Part two is promised.
topics: Stuff You Should Know true crime playlist

segments.title: Teaser
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a playlist pick about the 1982 Chicago-area poisoning deaths, noted as unsolved.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about movies, including Mandy and Blade Runner, before starting the recording.

segments.title: Setting the scene: 1982
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh recall major 1982 news events, including the Air Florida crash in the Potomac, the Wayne Williams conviction, the Pan Am 759 crash, and the Iowa paperboy disappearance, and set up the Tylenol story.

segments.title: Extra Strength Tylenol background
segments.summary: Explanation of Tylenol as the dominant over-the-counter pain reliever in 1982, holding about 37 percent of the market, and how it differs from aspirin.

segments.title: First victims: Mary Anne Kellerman and Adam Janis
segments.summary: Twelve-year-old Mary Anne Kellerman died after taking Extra Strength Tylenol for a sore throat on September 29, 1982. Later that morning Adam Janis, 27, died in Arlington Heights after taking Tylenol for chest pains; both were initially thought to have had strokes or heart attacks.

segments.title: Mary Reiner, Mary McFarlane, and the Janis family deaths
segments.summary: Mary Reiner died after feeling dizzy following childbirth; Mary McFarlane collapsed at an Illinois Bell store in Lombard after taking Tylenol for a headache. Stanley Janis, Adam's brother, collapsed at Adam's house after taking Tylenol, and his wife Teresa later collapsed but survived a couple of days.

segments.title: Live show aside
segments.summary: Hosts comment that the story is not suitable for live show material.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live shows

segments.title: Paula Prince
segments.summary: Flight attendant Paula Prince, 35, was found dead in her apartment on Friday after a welfare check; a bottle of Extra Strength Tylenol was open on the counter and receipts showed purchase on September 29.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Message break.

segments.title: Cyanide found in capsules
segments.summary: Medical examiner Michael Schaeffer tested the capsules and found potassium cyanide, about 65 milligrams, in place of acetaminophen; roughly 50 milligrams can kill a healthy adult. The hosts discuss how cyanide is detected and its history in executions.

segments.title: How cyanide kills
segments.summary: Explanation of cyanide binding to cytochrome c oxidase, blocking oxygen use by cells, shutting down the central nervous system, convulsions, cherry-red skin, and bitter almond odor.

segments.title: Early identification and citizen investigators
segments.summary: Within hours and days the link to Tylenol was made. Fire captain Philip Capitelli, whose mother-in-law knew the Kellerman family, investigated, and public health nurse Helen Jensen pushed for attention and joined forces with him.

segments.title: Donahue press conference and poison control calls
segments.summary: Cook County deputy chief medical examiner Edmund Donahue held a press conference warning people to stop taking Tylenol; poison control lines lit up, with advice that people still talking after a few minutes were likely fine.

segments.title: Mayor Byrne's response and nationwide reaction
segments.summary: Mayor Jane Byrne had flyers printed in several languages and police drove through neighborhoods with loudspeakers urging people not to take Tylenol. Coverage spread nationally and worldwide, and an October poll found 90 percent of respondents aware of the story.

segments.title: Copycat tampering and food scares
segments.summary: Around 270 product tampering reports followed in the month after, 36 of them hardcore tamperings. Copycat cases included Tylenol-like tampering of Sinex and Visine, a Colorado man poisoned with mercuric chloride, tampered orange juice and chocolate milk, and the Detroit ballpark hot dog razor blade hoax and recall.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Message break.

segments.title: Time magazine coverage and Task Force formation
segments.summary: Time described copycats as emulating a demonic hero. Local investigations were folded into a Tylenol Task Force including the FBI, Illinois State Police, and FDA, led by the Illinois state's attorney's office.

segments.title: Drag net and lot MC2880
segments.summary: Investigators searched stores within about a fifty-mile radius, finding more tainted bottles still on shelves. The tampered containers came from lot MC2880, distributed east of the Mississippi, but from different plants and stores, leading investigators to conclude the tampering happened in stores.

segments.title: Suspects and the mad poisoner theory
segments.summary: Theories included a disgruntled Johnson & Johnson employee, a serial killer, and a targeted killing; the mad poisoner theory, that a local person tampered with bottles in about seven hours across the Chicago area, became the main theory. Detective John 'Pinky' McFarland tested samples, and Johnson & Johnson tests found the lot pure.

segments.title: Mid-October tainted bottle
segments.summary: Another tainted bottle bought September 29 was found; a woman was nearly given it at a family gathering but her sister offered Bufferin instead.

segments.title: Part one wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts close part one, promise part two, and give contact info and credits.
